definition:
The new heavens and the new earth are the Bible's picture of the final state of all things: the whole created order, heaven and earth together, freed from the curse, cleansed of evil, and filled with the presence of God, who dwells with his people in it forever. The Bible's last hope is not that souls will leave the world for somewhere else, but that God will do for the world what he did for the body of Jesus: raise it, transform it, and keep it. In the Bible's language 'the heavens and the earth' means everything God made (Genesis 1:1), so a new heaven and a new earth means a new creation, not only a new sky. Christians have long spoken of the final destiny of the redeemed as 'heaven', and the New Testament does speak of an inheritance kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4) and of being with Christ at death; this study traces how the Bible places the final home of God's people in a creation where heaven and earth are joined.

Several words carry the doctrine. The Hebrew verb bara', 'to create', is used in its basic stem only with God as its subject, and Isaiah uses it for the future as well as the past: “I will create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). The adjective chadash, 'new', describes the new song, the new covenant, and the 'new thing' God is doing (Isaiah 43:19). In Greek, kainos, 'new', describes the new covenant, the new creation (kainē ktisis, 2 Corinthians 5:17), and the new heaven and earth of Revelation 21:1. Older handbooks drew a sharp line between kainos as 'new in kind' and neos as 'new in time'; the words do lean that way, but their meanings overlap, and the doctrine does not rest on the distinction. Jesus speaks of 'the renewal of all things' with the rare word palingenesia (Matthew 19:28), literally 'birth again', which Stoic philosophers used for the world's rebirth after its periodic burning and which Titus 3:5 uses for the new birth of a believer. Peter speaks of “the restoration of all things” (Acts 3:21), apokatastasis, a word used for restoring something to its proper condition.
ot:
The hope begins with the first creation. God makes the heavens and the earth, calls them good, and at the end of the sixth day “looked upon all that He had made, and indeed, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). He plants a garden, places the man in it, and walks there (Genesis 2:8; 3:8). Many scholars, including Gordon Wenham in a 1986 essay on sanctuary symbolism in the Eden story and G. K. Beale in The Temple and the Church's Mission (2004), have shown that Eden is described with the features of a sanctuary: the presence of God, the eastward entrance, the cherubim guarding it, the gold and precious stones, the river. The fall brings a curse on the ground itself: “cursed is the ground because of you” (Genesis 3:17), with thorns and thistles and toil, and the man and woman are driven out east of the garden. From then on the Bible's story is in large part the story of how God will again dwell with people on the earth. After the flood God makes his covenant not only with Noah but with “every living creature” and sets the rainbow as “a sign of the covenant between Me and the earth” (Genesis 9:13), which is the first sign that his commitment extends to the creation itself.

The tabernacle and the temple carry that promise forward. God tells Moses, “they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8), and the covenant promise takes its classic form: “I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (Leviticus 26:12). The sanctuary, with its cherubim, its lampstand shaped like a tree, and its images of fruit and flowers, recalls Eden in small. It is a pledge that God means to fill not one tent but the world. Even in the wilderness, when Israel refuses to enter the land, God swears “as surely as the whole earth is filled with the glory of the LORD” (Numbers 14:21), and the prophets make that the goal of history: “the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:14). The Psalms add that the renewal comes through judgment. When the LORD comes to judge the earth, the fields exult and “all the trees of the forest will sing for joy” (Psalm 96:12), because his judgment is the setting right of a spoiled world. Psalm 102 also says the heavens and earth “will perish” and wear out like clothing: “Like clothing You will change them” (Psalm 102:26), a line Hebrews 1:10-12 applies to Christ.

Isaiah gives the fullest vision. The coming son of David will judge the poor with righteousness, and then “The wolf will live with the lamb” and “They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water” (Isaiah 11:6, 9). The nations beat swords into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4; Micah 4:3), each person sits under his own vine and fig tree (Micah 4:4), the desert blossoms and the blind see and the lame leap (Isaiah 35:1-6), and God will make Zion's “wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD” (Isaiah 51:3). In Isaiah 60 the nations stream to Jerusalem's light, bringing their wealth, and the LORD himself replaces sun and moon as “your everlasting light” (Isaiah 60:19). Then comes the promise that gives the doctrine its name: “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered” (Isaiah 65:17). The picture that follows is earthy: no more weeping, houses built and lived in, vineyards planted and enjoyed, labor not in vain, and a restored peace among animals (Isaiah 65:18-25). It still speaks of death at a hundred years (Isaiah 65:20), which premillennial interpreters read as a description of the thousand-year reign before the final state, and others read as the prophet describing the unimaginable in the language of the best life his hearers could imagine, a life so long that dying at a hundred would seem to die young. Isaiah 66:22 promises that the new heavens and new earth “will endure before Me”.

Ezekiel ends his book with a vision of a restored temple from which a river flows east, growing deeper as it goes, turning the Dead Sea fresh, so that “wherever the river flows, everything will flourish” (Ezekiel 47:9), with trees along its banks whose “leaves will not wither” and whose leaves are “for healing” (Ezekiel 47:12). The city's name will be “THE LORD IS THERE” (Ezekiel 48:35). Zechariah pictures living water flowing out of Jerusalem and the day when “the LORD will become King over all the earth” (Zechariah 14:8-9). These visions are rooted in Israel's land, temple, and city, and Christians differ over how literally to take their details, but together they establish the shape the New Testament will complete: God's presence, a healed creation, the nations gathered, and the curse undone.
nt:
Jesus announced the kingdom of God and taught his disciples to pray for it to come “on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). He promised, “Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5), repeating Psalm 37:11, where the word means the land, and widening it. He spoke of “the renewal of all things, when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne” (Matthew 19:28), of many coming from east and west to feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matthew 8:11), and at the Last Supper of drinking the fruit of the vine “anew with you in My Father's kingdom” (Matthew 26:29). His healings were signs of the age to come breaking in. When John the Baptist asked whether he was the one, Jesus answered in the language of Isaiah 35 and 61: “The blind receive sight, the lame walk” (Matthew 11:5). John's Gospel presents Jesus himself as the new dwelling of God on earth, since “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14), and as the true temple (John 2:19-21). The resurrection happens in a garden on “the first day of the week” (John 20:1), and Mary takes the risen Jesus for the gardener (John 20:15); many readers see a deliberate echo of Genesis in these details, though John does not spell it out. What is plain is that the risen body of Jesus is the first piece of the new creation: a physical body, continuous with the one that was buried, raised beyond the reach of death.

The apostles spoke of the new creation as already begun and not yet complete. Peter told the crowd in the temple that heaven must receive Jesus “until the time comes for the restoration of all things, which God announced long ago through His holy prophets” (Acts 3:21). Paul says the promise to Abraham was that he would be “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), not only of Canaan. In Romans 8 he writes that “the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay and brought into the glorious freedom of the children of God” (Romans 8:21), and that it now groans “in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22), which is the groaning of something about to be born, not of something about to die. The new creation has already begun in the people who belong to Christ: “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17; Galatians 6:15). The scope of Christ's work is the whole of creation, since God was pleased “through Him to reconcile to Himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven” (Colossians 1:20) and to bring “all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ” (Ephesians 1:10). The goal is “that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

Two passages seem to point the other way, and they need careful reading. Hebrews speaks of Abraham looking for “the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (Hebrews 11:10), “a better country, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16), and of a final shaking that will remove “what can be shaken” so that “the unshakable may remain” (Hebrews 12:27). The heavenly city in Hebrews is not the opposite of the earth but the city that comes from God, and Revelation shows it coming down. 2 Peter 3 is more striking. The present heavens and earth “are reserved for fire” (2 Peter 3:7), and on the Day of the Lord “the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare” (2 Peter 3:10). The last phrase has a famous textual question. The oldest witnesses, the papyrus P72 and the fourth-century codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, read a verb meaning 'will be found', which modern translations render 'laid bare' or 'exposed'; many later manuscripts read 'will be burned up', which the King James Version follows; and the Nestle-Aland 28th edition (2012) prints 'will not be found', following a few early translations. Albert Wolters argued in 1987 that 'will be found' fits a refining image, fire that purifies metal and leaves what is genuine. Peter also compares the coming fire with the flood, through which “the world of that time perished” (2 Peter 3:6) though it was not annihilated, and he ends not with nothing but with “a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13).

Revelation closes the Bible with the fulfillment of every strand. John sees “a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more” (Revelation 21:1); in Revelation the sea is the realm of chaos from which the beast rises (Revelation 13:1), so its absence means there is nothing left to threaten. The direction of travel is striking: the holy city does not rise from the earth to heaven but comes “down out of heaven from God” (Revelation 21:2). The voice from the throne announces the covenant promise of Leviticus and Ezekiel in its final form: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3). God wipes away every tear, and “there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4). He says “Behold, I make all things new” (Revelation 21:5), not 'I make new things'. The city is a perfect cube (Revelation 21:16), the shape of the Most Holy Place in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:20), and it has no temple, “because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple” (Revelation 21:22): the whole city has become the place of God's presence. The nations walk by its light and “the kings of the earth will bring their glory” into it (Revelation 21:24), echoing Isaiah 60. Then Eden returns, enlarged into a city: the river of the water of life, the tree of life “for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:2), and “No longer will there be any curse” (Revelation 22:3). At the center is the vision of God himself: “They will see His face” (Revelation 22:4).

keyTexts.why: God sees everything he has made as very good. The new creation is the rescue of a good world, not the replacement of a bad one.
The ground is cursed because of human sin, bringing thorns, toil, and death. Revelation 22:3 answers it directly: no longer will there be any curse.
The heavens, earth, sea, fields, and trees rejoice because the LORD comes to judge the world in righteousness. Final judgment is good news for a creation spoiled by evil.
The Spirit-filled son of David brings justice, and peace spreads even among animals until the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD.
God promises to create new heavens and a new earth, a world of joy, secure homes, fruitful work, and peace. It supplies the language of Revelation 21.
A river flows from the temple and brings life wherever it goes, with trees whose leaves are for healing. Revelation 22 takes up the image.
Jesus speaks of the renewal of all things when the Son of Man sits on his throne. The word palingenesia pictures creation's rebirth.
Heaven receives Jesus until the restoration of all things spoken by the prophets. The ascension is not the end of God's plan for the earth.
Creation groans in the pains of childbirth and will be set free from its bondage to decay when God's children are revealed. The world's future is tied to the resurrection of the body.
Anyone in Christ is a new creation. The final renewal has already begun in the people who belong to the risen Christ.
All things were created through Christ, and through his cross God reconciles all things in heaven and on earth. Creation and new creation have the same Lord.
God will shake heaven and earth once more so that what cannot be shaken remains. The passage is central to the debate over renewal and replacement.
The present heavens and earth pass through fire, and believers look for a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells. Its textual question bears on how the fire is understood.
The new heaven and earth appear, the city comes down, God dwells with his people, and he makes all things new. The whole Bible's hope in one scene.
The river of life and the tree of life return, the curse is gone, and God's servants see his face. The Bible ends where it began, in a garden, now a city.

history:
The early church held the renewal of creation as part of its answer to the Gnostic teachers, who regarded the material world as the botched work of a lesser power. Irenaeus of Lyons (Against Heresies, about 180) argued in book 5 that the creation itself will be restored to its first condition and serve the righteous, and that what passes away is the present form of the world, not its substance (Against Heresies 5.36.1), reading 1 Corinthians 7:31. Augustine made the same distinction in The City of God (20.16, completed about 426): the world will pass away by being changed, not by being utterly destroyed, since it is the 'form' of this world that passes. Other Christians of the first centuries, including Papias, Justin, and Irenaeus, pictured a renewed earth of abundant fruitfulness during the thousand-year reign, and Augustine's reinterpretation of the millennium turned the Western church's attention toward heaven and the vision of God. Medieval theology gathered its hope around the beatific vision, the direct sight of God by the redeemed, which Thomas Aquinas treated as the final happiness of human beings, and Dante's Paradiso (completed about 1320) gave that hope its greatest poem. Medieval theologians still taught a renewal of the physical world after the judgment, but it stood at the edge of the picture rather than the center.

The Reformers kept both strands. John Calvin, commenting on Romans 8:21, taught that the creation will share in a better condition, while warning against curious speculation about its details. In the early seventeenth century the Lutheran theologian Johann Gerhard (1582-1637) argued in his Theological Commonplaces that at the end the present world, apart from human beings and angels, will be annihilated and a new one created, and some later Lutheran orthodox theologians followed him, while Reformed theologians generally taught that the world will be renewed. Puritan devotion, most famously Richard Baxter's The Saints' Everlasting Rest (1650), fixed the believer's longing on heaven, and much Protestant hymnody of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries spoke of the final home as a place beyond the world.

The renewal of creation returned to the center of Protestant theology through the Dutch Reformed tradition. Abraham Kuyper (1837-1920) and Herman Bavinck (1854-1921), whose Reformed Dogmatics ends with a long treatment of the renewal of creation, taught that grace restores nature rather than replacing it. Richard Mouw's When the Kings Come Marching In (1983) read Isaiah 60 and Revelation 21 as a promise that the good works of human culture will be purified and brought into the city of God. Anthony Hoekema's The Bible and the Future (1979), N. T. Wright's Surprised by Hope (2008), and J. Richard Middleton's A New Heaven and a New Earth (2014) made the case to a wide readership that the Bible's final hope is a renewed earth. Jürgen Moltmann's The Coming of God (German 1995) set out a cosmic eschatology in which all creation is drawn into God's future. Others have warned against losing the older emphasis: Hans Boersma's Seeing God (2018) argues that the vision of God, not the renewed earth, must remain the heart of the Christian hope. Eastern Orthodox theology has long spoken of the whole cosmos being transfigured by God's presence, with the transfiguration of Christ as its sign.

differ.body: The present heaven and earth will be purified, freed from the curse, and transformed, and this same creation will become the new creation. Defenders point out that Scripture's pattern is redemption, not replacement: the body that is raised is the body that was buried, and the creation that groans is the creation that will be set free (Romans 8:21). The flood is Peter's model for the coming fire, and the flood cleansed the world rather than abolishing it (2 Peter 3:6). The oldest reading of 2 Peter 3:10, 'will be found', suits a fire that tests and refines. God says “I make all things new” (Revelation 21:5), not 'I make new things'. This is the view of Irenaeus and Augustine, of the medieval theologians, and of most Reformed theologians, including Bavinck and Hoekema.

The present world will pass away completely and God will create a new one. Defenders read Scripture's strongest language in its plain force: the heavens “will perish” (Psalm 102:26; Hebrews 1:11), the first heaven and earth “had passed away” (Revelation 21:1), the elements will be destroyed by fire (2 Peter 3:10-12), and “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24:35). The shaking of Hebrews 12:27 removes created things so that only the unshakable remains. On this view the continuity between old and new lies in the people God saves, who are raised, not in the physical world, and the glory of the new creation is that it owes nothing to the old. Johann Gerhard and a number of Lutheran orthodox theologians of the seventeenth century taught that the world apart from human beings and angels will be annihilated.

differ.view: The vision of God at the center
differ.body: The final hope is above all to see God, the beatific vision, and the renewed creation is the setting for that sight rather than its substance. Defenders point to the climax of Revelation, “They will see His face” (Revelation 22:4), to Jesus' promise that the pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8), and to “we will see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2). They hold with Augustine, Aquinas, and the great tradition of Christian contemplation that nothing created can finally satisfy a creature made for God. They welcome the recovery of the renewed earth but warn that talk of new-creation culture, work, and politics can make the final state sound like this world improved, and lose the joy of God himself. Hans Boersma has made this case at length.

differ.view: The renewed earth and its culture
differ.body: The final hope is God dwelling with his people in a renewed, physical creation, where human life, work, and culture continue in a purified form. Defenders point to the earthiness of Isaiah 65, to the meek inheriting the earth (Matthew 5:5), to Romans 8, and to the kings of the earth bringing their glory and honor into the city (Revelation 21:24-26), which they read as the best of human cultures, cleansed and offered to God. The vision of God is real, they argue, but it happens in a creation, not instead of one, since God's dwelling place comes down to be with man (Revelation 21:3). Richard Mouw, N. T. Wright, and J. Richard Middleton are prominent defenders, standing in the tradition of Kuyper and Bavinck.

errors:
The church has rejected every teaching that treats matter itself as evil and salvation as escape from the created world. The Gnostic teachers of the second century, and later the Manichaeans whom Augustine once followed and then opposed, taught that the physical world was a prison or a mistake; the church answered with the goodness of creation, the incarnation, the bodily resurrection, and the renewal of all things. A softer form of the same error survives whenever Christians speak as if the earth will simply be thrown away and only souls matter. That picture cannot account for Romans 8, for the resurrection of the body, or for the city that comes down. It can also excuse indifference to the creation God called very good and to the bodily needs of neighbors.

The opposite error is to think the new creation can be built by human effort. The church has refused programs, religious or political, that identified their own society with the kingdom of God or promised to bring in the new world by law, revolution, or technology. The New Testament says the city comes down out of heaven from God; it is his gift at his coming, after judgment has removed evil, and nothing unclean will enter it (Revelation 21:27). The church also rejects any view that dissolves the distinction between God and the world, as if the new creation meant creation becoming God. God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28), but as Creator dwelling with his creatures, who see his face and serve him.
life:
If God intends to renew his creation rather than discard it, then what Christians do with the world now is not wasted. Care for land and animals, the making of beautiful and useful things, honest work, and the healing of bodies are not distractions from the gospel but signs that point to its end, although they do not bring it about. Paul's words that labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58) come at the end of a chapter about the resurrection of the body. The hope also teaches patience with the world's groaning. Christians need not pretend that creation is fine, and they need not despair of it; they can grieve its brokenness and still expect its healing.

The new creation also changes worship and hope. Every Lord's Supper is a small taste of the banquet Jesus promised to share anew in his Father's kingdom, bread and wine being fruits of the earth. Every prayer that God's kingdom come on earth as in heaven asks for the new creation. And the final picture keeps the whole hope personal: the best thing about the new world is not its river or its gates of pearl but that God dwells there, wipes away every tear, and his servants see his face.
questions: The Bible begins with a garden and ends with a city that contains a garden. What does that movement suggest about God's purposes for human work and culture?
How do you read passages like 2 Peter 3:10 and Hebrews 12:27, which speak of destruction and shaking, alongside Romans 8:21, which speaks of creation being set free?
If the final hope is a renewed creation where God dwells with his people, how should that shape the way Christians care for the earth, their bodies, and their neighbors now?
